replays.t: Card fraud: the winning Kaggle solution, rebuilt in seven versions
replays.note: IEEE-CIS Fraud Detection, Kaggle, July to October 2019. 6,381 teams. About 590,000 labelled card transactions, 3.5% of them fraud, around 450 columns with masked names. Scored by AUC. Chris Deotte's team came first with 0.9677 on the public board and 0.9459 on the private one. Everything below comes from his own account of it: NVIDIA's write-up. Data and late submissions: the competition page (needs a Kaggle account). A GPU makes each run minutes instead of hours; XGBoost uses it with device="cuda". The only scores quoted here are the ones the winners published. Your own numbers go in the boxes.

subs.t: Version 0: a validation you can trust
subs.about: Before any modelling idea, decide how you will know that an idea helped. The winners split by time, never at random, because the test set comes after the training set.

subs.about: Label-encode the categorical columns, then add frequency encodings (how often each value occurs), combined columns such as card1 with addr1, and parts split out of columns such as the cents of the amount. Add one idea at a time and keep it only if validation improves.

subs.about: For a group such as one card, add the mean and standard deviation of the amount within that group. A transaction far from its own group's habit is suspicious.

subs.t: Version 3: the client ID, the idea that won
subs.about: The winners worked out which transactions belong to one client and built an ID from card1, addr1 and the day minus D1. The write-up gives the line of code but not the reasoning; D1 behaves like a count of days since a client was first seen, which would make the difference fixed for a client, and checking that against the data is part of this version. They built group statistics over the ID and did not give the ID itself to the model, to avoid overfitting. Their local validation went from 0.9363 to 0.9472 at this step.

subs.t: Version 4: drop features that do not survive time
subs.about: For each feature alone, train on the first month and test on the last. A feature that cannot beat 0.5 there describes the past, not fraud. The winners tested 242 features this way and removed 19.

replays.t: A racing car that learns: reward design, the way a winning DeepRacer team did it
replays.note: AWS DeepRacer League, on the re:Invent 2018 track. An AWS blog post (April 2022, in Chinese) compares three reward strategies by one team. A centre-line reward was trained for 12 hours and then failed on the physical track, which the authors put down to overfitting. A pure-pursuit reward reached full laps in simulation after about 3 hours and was one of the few that finished the physical track. With it they won: 44 s in round one, then 38.74 s, and 34 s in an exhibition run. A third strategy that followed a computed racing line went off the track in simulation. DeepRacer itself now runs on paid AWS services, so this replay uses a free stand-in: the CarRacing environment in Gymnasium, on your own machine (pip install "gymnasium[box2d]"). It is not the same simulator, so their lap times are not targets. What transfers is the lesson about rewards. AWS's own reward function examples are worth reading beside it.

about.frontier:
This is a snapshot taken on 10 October 2026. The titles and links were collected from Hugging Face's trending page, one round-up article and a search. Nobody has read these papers for you, and trending is not the same as important. The list is here so that you practise the skill that matters: deciding in fifteen minutes what a paper is worth.

For each one, tick it when you have done these three things:

  1. Read the title, the abstract and every figure. Nothing else.
  2. Write one line in your notes: what do they claim, compared with what, and measured how?
  3. Decide: skip, keep an eye on, or replicate. Most are a skip, and saying so is the skill.

A paper you decide to replicate moves to the Papers list, where the routine is read, implement, reproduce. The papers there are the ones the whole field stands on; do those first.

A new snapshot arrives with each content update. The old one stays, so your ticks keep their meaning.
about.replays:
Three competitions that were won, each rebuilt as a ladder of versions. You start with a plain baseline and add one of the winners' ideas at a time, measuring after each. That is how they got there, and it is also what an interviewer wants to hear: not "I used XGBoost" but "this change moved validation from here to here, and this is why".

Rules for a replay:

  • Write your score in the box under each version before you start the next. The row of numbers is the result.
  • Read the winners' account for an idea, then close it and write the code yourself. The rule about typing every line applies here too.
  • The scores quoted are the ones the winners published. Where they published none for a step, none is given.

Do them in order of the stages: fraud after Stage 3, the science exam after Stage 5, the racing car after Stage 6. Expect each one to take a few weeks of evenings. Each is a portfolio project once it is written up.
about.video:
The chapters of 70 Leetcode problems in 5+ hours (every data structure) by stoney codes, in the video's own order. "Watch" opens the video at that chapter, and "LeetCode" opens the problem. Both need a connection.

Where it says Solve here, this app has a problem on the same idea that works offline, with tests, hints and a solution. The statement is this app's own, so details differ from LeetCode. Solving it here ticks the row.

How to use a walkthrough video without wasting it: read the problem, pause, and try for twenty minutes first. Watch the solution only after that, then close the video and write it again from memory.
about.watch:
This list is built from your own YouTube subscriptions: 111 channels, read on 10 October 2026. Almost every row comes from a channel you already follow, and its playlist or video link was read from that channel's own pages the same day. The few rows marked not subscribed are lecture series from elsewhere that the plan leans on.

How to use it:

  • One series per stage is enough. The row marked start here in each section is the one to open first. The rest are for when that one does not suit you.
  • Attempt first, watch second. A video is the hint after your twenty minutes, not the lesson before them. For the from-scratch videos especially, write your own version before you watch theirs.
  • Tick a row when you have built what it teaches, not when you have watched it.
  • The same rows appear on the skill pages of the Map, two to four per skill, so you rarely need to come here to find one.

Watching feels like progress and is the cheapest part of learning. If a week has more hours of video than of typing, the week went wrong.

Subscribed channels that have no row here

  • News, podcasts and commentary. Good company over dinner; they do not count as a session: Two Minute Papers, Machine Learning Street Talk, Dwarkesh Patel, Lex Fridman, 1littlecoder, Fireship, Developers Digest, The PrimeTime, ThePrimeagen, Siraj Raval, Computerphile, FloatHeadPhysics.
  • Company and institution channels. Search them when you need one specific talk: Google, Google for Developers, Google TechTalks, Microsoft Research, Meta Open Source, Intel Devs, Visual Studio Code, Harvard University, San Diego Machine Learning, Consensus.
  • Useful, but they repeat what a row above already covers: GeeksforGeeks, William Lin (tmwilliamlin168), Daniel Bourke, Aleksa Gordić - The AI Epiphany, Siddhardhan, BrainOmega, PyImageSearch, Murtaza's Workshop - Robotics and AI, TileStats, Data Science Analytics, Luis Serrano Academy, Radu Mariescu-Istodor, Python Tutorials for Digital Humanities, Kola Olayinka, Blitz Kim, Cracking Concepts by Kiran Mary Matthew.
  • Outside this plan: Zerodha Varsity, Nick Chapsas, Amichai Mantinband, Vasilios Syrakis.
  • Could not be placed, because the channel shows no playlists to judge by: Andrew Hu.
about.syl:
This list follows the core courses of the M.Tech in Computational and Data Science at NITK, from the curriculum for 2019-20 onwards. It has three kinds of row.

  • Explain from memory. A topic from the course. Tick it when you can explain it in four or five lines with no notes. The app then asks you to write those lines, and brings them back under Recall.
  • Write it here. An exercise in this app. The row ticks itself when the exercise passes.
  • Run it on a real machine. A program to write and time on the V100 or your own computer. The app cannot run these. Tick one when you have the numbers written down.

The electives are not followed course by course, because which ones you take is your choice. Where the app already overlaps one:

ElectiveWhat the app has
MA841 Cloud Computing, MA855 Big Data AnalyticsThe MapReduce exercises and lesson, and the MLOps quiz topic. Nothing on virtualisation, storage systems or Spark itself
MA842 Distributed Computing SystemsMessage passing and deadlock in the third systems lesson, and the federated learning quiz topic. Nothing on clocks, global state or mutual exclusion
MA845 Computational Linear AlgebraThe Linear systems skill, the Sparse and structured matrices skill, and the linear algebra quiz topic
MA853 Pattern Recognition, MA854 Statistical Techniques for Data MiningThe machine learning quiz topic and the Classic ML skill
MA847 Soft ComputingNeural networks, under Neural nets from scratch and the deep learning quiz topic. Nothing on fuzzy logic or genetic algorithms
MA844 Advanced Data ScienceThe best-fit direction exercise. Nothing on streaming, topic models or wavelets

The othersNothing

Content is versioned, so an elective can be added later without touching your progress.
